metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Critical equipment lead times, not just permits, now gate data center construction: order-to-delivery for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators has stretched from months to years.

The pattern is a shift in where the constraint sits. A data center is electrical and thermal plant before it is a building full of compute, and the schedule for that plant is set by manufacturing queues rather than by site work. When those queues run long, the date a facility can energize stops being a construction question and becomes a procurement one.

For AI specifically, this puts a physical interval between the decision to add compute and the ability to run it. Accelerators appear in the same lead-time list as transformers and switchgear, so the silicon and the infrastructure that feeds it can be scarce on the same schedule. Capacity planning that assumes power and cooling arrive on demand will misjudge when new compute actually comes online.

What this does not establish is magnitude. It gives a direction, months to years, without current lead times, ranges by equipment type, or regional variation, and it does not say whether the stretch is continuing, plateauing, or reversing. Hyperscaler and colocation capital expenditure and colocation rental rates are tracked alongside it in the same financials and supply chain category, which suggests equipment queues, spending, and rents are meant to be read together, but nothing here shows that relationship, only that the three are watched side by side.
